prompt.context_jp: 夏の夕暮れ、花咲家の食卓には父・幸三の手料理___並んでいた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 夏の夕暮れ、花咲家の食卓には父・幸三の手料理___並んでいた。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that fits: the sentence introduces what was on the table as new scene information.

feedback.correct_en: The topic is already set with 食卓には (on the table). What appears there — 手料理 — is new information being introduced to the scene, so が is natural.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would re-topicalize 手料理, which clashes with the scene-setting 食卓には already acting as topic. を doesn't fit 並ぶ (an intransitive verb here).

contrast_examples.jp: 机の上に本が置いてある。
contrast_examples.en: There's a book on the desk. (new info)

contrast_examples.jp: その本は机の上にある。
contrast_examples.en: That book is on the desk. (topic known)

prompt.context_jp: 箸を動かしながら、舞___ぼんやりと壁のカレンダーを眺めている。
prompt.prompt_jp: 舞___ぼんやりと壁のカレンダーを眺めている。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks Mai here as the ongoing topic of the scene?

feedback.correct_en: Mai is the established topic of the chapter — the narrator is describing what she, the known protagonist, is doing. は signals topic continuity.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would present Mai as newly identified ('it is Mai who...'), which would sound like she's being introduced for the first time.

contrast_examples.jp: 舞は雑誌を読んでいる。
contrast_examples.en: Mai (as topic) is reading a magazine.

contrast_examples.jp: 誰が読んでいるの？—舞が読んでいる。
contrast_examples.en: Who's reading? — Mai is. (identifying new info)

prompt.context_jp: そのとき、背後から見慣れた人影___近づいてきた。
prompt.prompt_jp: そのとき、背後から見慣れた人影___近づいてきた。
prompt.prompt_en: A figure appears for the first time in the scene. Which particle introduces this new element?

feedback.correct_en: The figure (相馬) is being newly introduced into the scene — classic new-information が, often used for narrative appearances.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would wrongly treat the figure as already-known topic. を is wrong because 近づく is intransitive.

contrast_examples.jp: 向こうから子供が走ってきた。
contrast_examples.en: A child came running from over there.

contrast_examples.jp: その子供は笑っていた。
contrast_examples.en: That child (now known) was laughing.

prompt.context_jp: 何ですか？ その哀れむような上から目線___
prompt.prompt_jp: その哀れむような上から目線___
prompt.prompt_en: Mai is calling out Souma's look as the topic of her complaint. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: She's picking up 'that pitying look' as the topic she wants to comment on — は is natural for 'as for that look of yours...'
feedback.incorrect_en: が would present the look as newly discovered information, but Mai is clearly commenting on something she's already noticed.

contrast_examples.jp: その言い方は何ですか。
contrast_examples.en: What's with that way of speaking?

contrast_examples.jp: 誰かの声がする。
contrast_examples.en: I hear someone's voice. (new perception)

prompt.context_jp: 1人旅の何___悪いんですか？
prompt.prompt_jp: 1人旅の何___悪いんですか？
prompt.prompt_en: Mai is challenging Souma — 'what (exactly) is bad about solo travel?' Which particle fits a question seeking new information?

feedback.correct_en: Interrogatives like 何 asking to identify something always take が, because the answer is new/identifying information.
feedback.incorrect_en: 何は悪いんですか sounds unnatural — you can't topicalize an unknown 'what.'

contrast_examples.jp: 誰が来ましたか。
contrast_examples.en: Who came?

contrast_examples.jp: 何がおかしいの？
contrast_examples.en: What's funny?

prompt.context_jp: 臨店班の次長として上に仕える芝崎___、常に上層部の顔色に気を配っている男だ。
prompt.prompt_jp: 臨店班の次長として上に仕える芝崎___、常に上層部の顔色に気を配っている男だ。
prompt.prompt_en: The narrator is describing Shibazaki as a general character trait. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: This is a characterizing statement — 'As for Shibazaki, he is a man who...' は fits the topic-comment description.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make it sound like identifying 'who the man is', not characterizing Shibazaki himself.

contrast_examples.jp: 父は厳しい人だ。
contrast_examples.en: My father is a strict person.

contrast_examples.jp: 厳しいのが父だ。
contrast_examples.en: The strict one is my father. (identifying)

prompt.context_jp: 真藤常務に 次期頭取争いの ライバル___出現って 行内で もう 話題になってんのに！
prompt.prompt_jp: 次期頭取争いの ライバル___出現
prompt.prompt_en: A rival has appeared — the rival is new information to the discourse. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: The rival's appearance is the hot new piece of gossip — が marks this new, surprising information.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would presuppose that the rival is already a known topic, which contradicts 'you don't know?'

contrast_examples.jp: 新しい社長が決まった。
contrast_examples.en: A new president has been decided. (news)

contrast_examples.jp: 新しい社長は厳しい人だ。
contrast_examples.en: The new president is a strict person. (already known)

prompt.context_jp: 頭取争いという言葉___、窓口に立っていた自分にはやはり遠い世界の話に思える。
prompt.prompt_jp: 頭取争いという言葉___、窓口に立っていた自分にはやはり遠い世界の話に思える。
prompt.prompt_en: The phrase 'presidential competition' is being set up as the topic of what follows. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: は sets up 'the phrase 頭取争い' as a topic and comments on how it feels to Mai — a classic topic-comment structure.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would present the phrase as newly identified subject of a factual event, not as something being evaluated.

contrast_examples.jp: その言葉は彼女にとって重かった。
contrast_examples.en: Those words were heavy for her.

contrast_examples.jp: 急に大きな声がした。
contrast_examples.en: Suddenly there was a loud voice. (event)

prompt.context_jp: 真藤___陰で何を企てているのか、堂島はとうに見抜いているのかもしれない。
prompt.prompt_jp: 真藤___陰で何を企てているのか
prompt.prompt_en: Inside the embedded question 'what Shindo is plotting,' which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: In embedded 疑問 clauses (何を...のか), the subject is typically marked with が, since it's part of the content being questioned.
feedback.incorrect_en: は tends to escape the subordinate clause and sound like contrastive topic, which is awkward here.

contrast_examples.jp: 誰が来るか分からない。
contrast_examples.en: I don't know who will come.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は何を考えているのか分からない。
contrast_examples.en: I don't know what he's thinking. (he = outer topic)

prompt.context_jp: 臨店班が騒ぎを起こせば、そのとばっちりを受けるの___自分たちだという思いもある。
prompt.prompt_jp: そのとばっちりを受けるの___自分たちだ
prompt.prompt_en: 'The ones who take the hit = us.' Which particle creates this exhaustive-identification reading?

feedback.correct_en: The 〜のは〜だ cleft construction puts the known situation as topic (は) and identifies 'us' as the answer. This is the standard focus-cleft frame.
feedback.incorrect_en: 〜のが〜だ is possible but marked; here the natural pattern is のは…だ because 'taking the hit' is the given premise.

contrast_examples.jp: 悪いのは私です。
contrast_examples.en: The one at fault is me.

contrast_examples.jp: 困るのは子供だ。
contrast_examples.en: The one who suffers is the child.

prompt.context_jp: 繁忙期の支店の空気___、かつてテラーだった舞にはなじみ深いものだった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 繁忙期の支店の空気___、かつてテラーだった舞にはなじみ深いものだった。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle sets up 'the branch atmosphere' as the topic being commented on?

feedback.correct_en: The sentence comments on how the atmosphere feels to Mai — a topic-comment pattern. は fits.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would announce the atmosphere as a new fact, not as the subject being described.

contrast_examples.jp: この街は静かだ。
contrast_examples.en: This town is quiet. (comment)

contrast_examples.jp: 急に風が吹いた。
contrast_examples.en: A wind suddenly blew. (event)

prompt.context_jp: 支店の裏手のベンチに、スーツ姿の若い男___一人で腰を下ろしているのが見えた。
prompt.prompt_jp: スーツ姿の若い男___一人で腰を下ろしているのが見えた。
prompt.prompt_en: A young man is spotted — he is newly introduced to the scene. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: Perception verb constructions ('I saw X doing Y') introduce X as new information inside the complement — が is required.
feedback.incorrect_en: は inside a 〜のが見えた complement is ungrammatical; the inner subject must be marked with が.

contrast_examples.jp: 猫が走っているのが見えた。
contrast_examples.en: I saw a cat running.

contrast_examples.jp: 鳥が鳴くのが聞こえる。
contrast_examples.en: I can hear a bird singing.

prompt.context_jp: でかい ため息___ ここまで聞こえたぞ
prompt.prompt_jp: でかい ため息___ ここまで聞こえたぞ
prompt.prompt_en: Souma teases Matsuki about a sigh — presented as a new, perceivable event. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: 聞こえる takes が for what is heard — and the sigh is a newly noticed phenomenon.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would wrongly treat the sigh as a known topic. を is wrong — 聞こえる is intransitive (you don't 'hear X' with を).

contrast_examples.jp: 外で音がした。
contrast_examples.en: There was a sound outside.

contrast_examples.jp: 遠くで鐘が鳴るのが聞こえる。
contrast_examples.en: I can hear a bell ringing far away.

prompt.context_jp: 大きく儲けてるわけ___ないんですが 黒字です
prompt.prompt_jp: 大きく儲けてるわけ___ないんですが
prompt.prompt_en: Matsuki contrasts 'not big profits' with 'but we are in the black.' Which particle marks the contrastive focus?

feedback.correct_en: わけではない is the set negation pattern, with は providing contrastive focus: 'it's not that we're making huge profits, but...'
feedback.incorrect_en: がは and をは are not valid particle combinations in Japanese.

contrast_examples.jp: 嫌いなわけではない。
contrast_examples.en: It's not that I dislike it.

contrast_examples.jp: 全部できたわけじゃない。
contrast_examples.en: It's not that I finished everything.

prompt.context_jp: 業績のいい勝ち組___融資する
prompt.prompt_jp: 業績のいい勝ち組___融資する
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks the recipient of the loan here?

feedback.correct_en: 融資する takes に for the party receiving the loan — 'lend to the winners.'
feedback.incorrect_en: を would mark the loan amount, not the recipient. が is wrong — the winners aren't the subject of 融資する.

contrast_examples.jp: 中小企業に融資する。
contrast_examples.en: Lend to a small-to-mid-size company.

contrast_examples.jp: 大金を融資する。
contrast_examples.en: Lend a large sum of money.

prompt.context_jp: また余計なことに ___を突っ込んで マズイ問題とか見つけちゃうと アレだから
prompt.prompt_jp: また余計なことに ___を突っ込んで
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the body-part noun that fits the idiom 'to poke one's nose into / meddle.'

feedback.correct_en: 首を突っ込む ('stick one's neck in') is the set idiom for meddling in something you shouldn't be involved in — exactly Shibazaki's worry.
feedback.incorrect_en: 顔を出す means 'to show up briefly' (not meddle), and 頭を突っ込む isn't a standard idiom in this sense.

contrast_examples.jp: 他人のことに首を突っ込むな。
contrast_examples.en: Don't stick your nose in other people's business.

contrast_examples.jp: ちょっと顔を出してきた。
contrast_examples.en: I just stopped by for a moment.

prompt.context_jp: お父さん 傷口に___を 塗るようなこと言っちゃったかな？
prompt.prompt_jp: 傷口に___を 塗るようなこと
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the word that completes the Japanese idiom equivalent to 'rub salt in the wound.'

feedback.correct_en: 傷口に塩を塗る = 'rub salt into the wound,' used when you say something that makes a painful situation worse — perfect for Kozo's teasing moment.
feedback.incorrect_en: The idiom specifically uses 塩 (salt). 油 would evoke 'adding fuel to the fire' (火に油), a different idiom.

contrast_examples.jp: 傷口に塩を塗るな。
contrast_examples.en: Don't rub salt in the wound.

contrast_examples.jp: 火に油を注ぐ。
contrast_examples.en: Pour oil on the fire. (make it worse)

prompt.context_jp: 貸すだけ貸しといて 突然 容赦なく___を外す
prompt.prompt_jp: 突然 容赦なく___を外す
prompt.prompt_en: Which word completes the idiom 'to pull the ladder out from under someone' (abandon them suddenly)?

feedback.correct_en: ハシゴを外す literally 'remove the ladder' — leaving someone stranded after helping them up. It's exactly what Azumi feels the bank is doing.
feedback.incorrect_en: The other words don't form idioms in Japanese for this betrayal/abandonment image.

contrast_examples.jp: 途中でハシゴを外された。
contrast_examples.en: I got the ladder pulled out mid-way.

contrast_examples.jp: 見捨てられた気分だ。
contrast_examples.en: I feel abandoned.

prompt.context_jp: 銀行が黒字の取引先から融資を強引に回収することを指す言葉。
prompt.prompt_jp: これって ___ですよね？
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the term Mai uses for a bank forcibly withdrawing loans from a healthy client.

feedback.correct_en: 貸し剥がし specifically names the predatory act of 'peeling off' loans from borrowers who are performing — the chapter's key accusation.
feedback.incorrect_en: 貸し出し just means 'lending.' 貸し倒れ means a bad debt (the lender's loss), not the forcible recall of a healthy loan.

contrast_examples.jp: 銀行が貸し剥がしに走る。
contrast_examples.en: The bank resorts to loan-pulling.

contrast_examples.jp: 貸し倒れが発生した。
contrast_examples.en: A bad debt occurred.

prompt.context_jp: 相馬が引き返したがらない中、松木が言う。
prompt.prompt_jp: ___船ですよ 相馬さん
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrase completes the idiom meaning 'we're already in this — can't back out now'?

feedback.correct_en: 乗りかかった船 — 'a ship you've already boarded' — the idiom for being committed to a task once begun.
feedback.incorrect_en: 降りた/沈んだ don't form this idiom and would convey the opposite (getting off / sinking).

contrast_examples.jp: 乗りかかった船だから最後までやる。
contrast_examples.en: I'm already on board, so I'll see it through.

contrast_examples.jp: 途中で降りるわけにはいかない。
contrast_examples.en: I can't get off halfway.

prompt.context_jp: 相馬が若い松木に残した信条。
prompt.prompt_jp: 俺たち銀行が___のは金だが 接するのは人だ
prompt.prompt_en: Which verb fits 'what we handle is money, but who we deal with is people'?

feedback.correct_en: 扱う ('handle/deal in') is the standard verb for what a profession or business works with — 'What banks handle is money, but what they interact with is people.'
feedback.incorrect_en: 数える ('count') is too literal, and 持つ ('hold/possess') misses the sense of 'professionally deal in.'

contrast_examples.jp: この店では和菓子を扱っている。
contrast_examples.en: This shop deals in Japanese sweets.

contrast_examples.jp: 金を数える。
contrast_examples.en: Count money. (literal action)

prompt.context_jp: カミングマートのやり方の説明。
prompt.prompt_jp: 赤字覚悟の___をして 競合店を そこから 撤退させる
prompt.prompt_en: Which word fits — Coming Mart's strategy of 'willingly losing money to drive out competitors'?

feedback.correct_en: 安売り (price-cutting / dumping) at a loss is precisely the predatory tactic Matsuki describes.
feedback.incorrect_en: 値上げ (raising prices) is the opposite move. 買い物 (shopping) is from the customer's side.

contrast_examples.jp: 赤字覚悟の安売りを続ける。
contrast_examples.en: Keep selling at a loss on purpose.

contrast_examples.jp: 原価割れで売る。
contrast_examples.en: Sell below cost.

prompt.context_jp: 父・幸三が娘にからかうように夕食で尋ねる台詞。
prompt.prompt_jp: どちらが父親の砕けた口調として自然ですか？
prompt.prompt_en: Which line sounds more natural as a father teasing his daughter casually at dinner?

choices.text: なんだ 舞 夏休み 予定のひとつもないのか？
どうしましたか 舞さん 夏休みのご予定はおありでしょうか？

feedback.correct_en: The chapter uses the blunt, affectionate なんだ...〜のか? form — appropriate for a father speaking casually to his adult daughter at home.
feedback.incorrect_en: The polite 〜でしょうか form would sound bizarrely formal between family members at the dinner table.

contrast_examples.jp: なんだ、元気ないのか？
contrast_examples.en: What's up, feeling down? (casual family)

contrast_examples.jp: お元気がないようですが。
contrast_examples.en: You seem unwell. (formal, distant)

prompt.context_jp: 支店長・中北が、本部から来た臨店班に対して言う挨拶。
prompt.prompt_jp: 支店長が本部の人間に礼を言う場面として、より自然な言い方は？
prompt.prompt_en: Which sounds more natural when a branch manager thanks visitors from headquarters?

choices.text: わざわざ 本部の方に ご足労いただいて すいませんでした
わざわざ 本部の人を 歩かせて 悪かったね

feedback.correct_en: ご足労いただく is the standard polite set phrase for thanking someone who came in person on your behalf — right register for a branch manager addressing HQ staff.
feedback.incorrect_en: 歩かせて悪かった is far too casual and would sound rude from a branch manager to visiting headquarters staff.

contrast_examples.jp: ご足労おかけしました。
contrast_examples.en: Thank you for coming all this way. (polite)

contrast_examples.jp: 来てくれてありがとう。
contrast_examples.en: Thanks for coming. (casual)

prompt.context_jp: 相馬が、気色ばむ支店長に対して意見を述べ始める場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 相馬が支店長に異論を切り出すのに自然な言い方は？
prompt.prompt_en: Which opening sounds more natural when politely pushing back against a superior?

choices.text: 失礼は承知で申し上げます
ちょっと言わせてもらうけど

feedback.correct_en: 失礼は承知で申し上げます ('I know this is impertinent, but...') is the humble business-polite frame for raising an objection to a superior — matches Souma's actual line.
feedback.incorrect_en: The casual ちょっと言わせてもらうけど would sound confrontational and inappropriate from a visiting inspector to a branch manager.

contrast_examples.jp: 恐れ入りますが、一つよろしいでしょうか。
contrast_examples.en: Pardon me, may I say one thing?

contrast_examples.jp: ちょっと言わせて。
contrast_examples.en: Let me say something. (casual)

prompt.context_jp: 相馬が松木の嘆きに同意する言い方。
prompt.prompt_jp: どちらが自然ですか？
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing sounds more natural for 'well, it can't be helped if they call it that'?

choices.text: そう言われても しかたがないみたいだな
そう言われても できないみたいだな

feedback.correct_en: 〜てもしかたがない is the natural collocation for 'can't be helped / nothing to say against it.' The bank really does deserve the label 貸し剥がし here.
feedback.incorrect_en: できない means 'cannot do' — a different meaning entirely; it doesn't fit this concession pattern.

contrast_examples.jp: 文句を言われてもしかたがない。
contrast_examples.en: Can't blame them for complaining.

contrast_examples.jp: そう言われてもどうにもできない。
contrast_examples.en: Even if told that, I can't do anything about it.

prompt.context_jp: 病院で寝ているように促す舞に、安積が「寝ている時間はない」と答える場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: より自然な舞の返し方は？
prompt.prompt_en: Which response by Mai sounds more natural when urging the collapsed Azumi to rest?

choices.text: 今日のところは 先生の言うことを聞いてください！
今日ぐらいは 先生の言うことを聞いてよ！

feedback.correct_en: 〜てください keeps appropriate distance with a company president she just met, while 今日のところは softens it to 'at least for today.' This matches the actual line.
feedback.incorrect_en: 〜聞いてよ is intimate casual speech, inappropriate from a bank employee to a patient they barely know, however urgent the situation.

contrast_examples.jp: 今日のところはお休みください。
contrast_examples.en: Please rest at least for today. (polite)

contrast_examples.jp: 今日は休みなよ。
contrast_examples.en: Just take today off. (close friends)
